approved: Private Health Insurance Legislation Amendment (Base Premium) Bill 2013

Proposed indexing the government's private health insurance rebate contribution to a base premium figure rather than actual premiums, noting the rebate costs around $5 billion a year and grows at an unsustainable 6.3 per cent, and said one hundred and twenty thousand people joined private health insurance in the six months after means testing began, with 54.6 per cent of the population holding some cover as of December 2012.

Defended private health insurance against the bills, saying the health system will cost $65 billion, or 16 per cent of the Commonwealth budget, in 2013 to 2014, noted over 96 per cent of his Bradfield constituents hold private health insurance, and said the changes would raise premiums by up to 27.5 per cent for 1.1 million Australians.

Rejected the bills, citing 84.5 per cent of voters in his Kooyong electorate, more than 105,000 people, hold private health insurance, and noted private hospitals provide nearly 40 per cent of hospital services nationally while public hospital spending rose 110 per cent under the Howard government between 1996 and 2007.

Criticised the bills, noting 53 per cent of her Solomon electorate's constituents hold private health insurance despite a median age of 32, and cited Royal Darwin Hospital's own figures showing only 54 per cent of emergency patients were seen within four hours against a 69 per cent target, with median surgery wait times of 49 days against a 31-day national average.

Argued against the bills, saying over 72,000 people in her McPherson electorate hold private hospital cover, and cited figures showing the rebate helped an additional eight million patients be treated in private hospitals over the past decade, saving taxpayers $26 billion.

Tallied Labor's rebate cuts at nearly $4 billion including $386 million from the lifetime health cover changes and $2.8 billion from means testing, and said close to 60 per cent of residents in her Macquarie electorate hold private health insurance.

Argued that the bill would make private health care more expensive and complex, criticised its rushed consideration, and said changes affecting Lifetime Health Cover would burden families and retirees while increasing pressure on public hospitals.

Argued that the bills would increase costs, reduce private health insurance coverage and shift patients into public hospitals, criticising the measures as budget-driven and harmful to regional services, while supporting greater cooperation between public and private providers.

Argued that the bill would increase private health insurance costs and complexity, damage coverage and increase demand for public hospitals, while criticising its rushed passage and the government's economic management.

Opposed the private health insurance bills, quoting the Prime Minister's earlier iron-clad guarantee to maintain the rebate, noted about 83 per cent of her Higgins electorate holds private cover, and cited Private Health Insurance Administration Council data showing $1.2 billion in prepayments to beat the changes, arguing the government is stripping more than $4 billion from a system used by 12.5 million Australians, including 5.6 million earning under $50,000 a year.

Summed up the debate, defending the Base Premium bill as funding commitments including $1,000 of dental care per child under the Grow Up Smiling program for 3.4 million children on family tax benefit A and DisabilityCare Australia, and accused the opposition of taking five different positions on private health insurance within a month.

Two parliamentary committee reports were presented: one on the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2013 Measures No. 1) Bill 2013 and one on the Private Health Insurance Legislation Amendment (Base Premium) Bill 2013, with both reports ordered to be printed.

The coalition argued that Labor’s changes to private health insurance broke repeated promises to maintain the rebate, and will increase premiums by up to 27.5 percent and push people onto public hospitals. The coalition moved an amendment to oppose the lifetime health cover component of the first bill and did not oppose the base premium bill.

The remaining stages of the Private Health Insurance Amendment (Lifetime Health Cover Loading and Other Measures) Bill 2012 and the Private Health Insurance Legislation Amendment (Base Premium) Bill 2013 were agreed to, and both bills were read a third time and passed.
Private Health Insurance Legislation Amendment (Base Premium) Act 2013
